analysis.one_liner: Taxes drug companies up to 100% of revenue from prescription drug price spikes.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a vote: it was referred to the Senate Finance Committee on the day it was introduced and stayed there until the Congress ended two years later.
analysis.plain_summary: The Stop Price Gouging Act would tax pharmaceutical companies on revenue they earn from raising prescription drug prices faster than overall inflation. If a company raised a drug's price above the chained Consumer Price Index, it would owe an excise tax of 50% to 100% of the extra revenue from the increase, depending on how big the spike was, with an allowance for genuine rises in manufacturing costs. Companies would have to report drug prices and sales each quarter to the HHS Inspector General, which could exempt drugs with legitimate reasons for increases and cheap drugs with multiple competitors. The extra revenue would fund NIH drug research.
analysis.who_benefits: People who rely on prescription drugs, especially those covered by Medicare, Medicaid, and other federal health programs, which the bill targets. The bill is designed to deter sudden large price increases and would send any tax collected to the National Institutes of Health.

how_it_helps.text: Imposes an excise tax equal to 50%, 75%, or 100% of the revenue a company gains from a drug price increase that exceeds the chained CPI, escalating with the size of the spike (50% up to 15%, 75% up to 20%, 100% at 20% or more).

Also applies to slow but persistent increases: if a drug's cumulative price rise over two to five years exceeds inflation by set thresholds, a cumulative tax of 50% to 100% applies, so companies cannot spread a large increase over several years to dodge the annual rule.

Adjusts the tax to exclude revenue gains attributable solely to higher input costs, and lets the HHS Secretary exempt drugs with legitimate for-cause increases and low-cost drugs (under $10 for a 30-day supply) sold by at least three competitors.

Requires quarterly public reporting of drug prices, unit sales, and revenues to the HHS Inspector General, with civil penalties of 0.5% to 1% of a drug's annual revenue per day for failure to report, and requires a GAO study of how launch prices for new drugs are set.
Authorizes appropriations equal to the revenue raised for NIH research and development of drugs.

analysis.who_pays: Brand-name pharmaceutical companies that raise drug prices faster than inflation. The tax is on their revenue from the price spike itself, not on patients directly.

drawbacks.text: An excise tax of this size gives companies an incentive to set higher initial launch prices for new drugs, which are not covered by the price-spike rules, and to weigh price increases against lost sales, so the benefit to patients is uncertain.
The tax applies only to drugs covered by federal health care programs, so patients with private insurance outside those programs get less direct protection.

Enforcement depends heavily on companies self-reporting quarterly data and on the Inspector General's judgment about input costs and exemptions, which creates room for disputes and delay; companies get notice and a hearing before any report goes to the IRS.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill targets a well-defined abuse—raising prices on existing drugs far faster than inflation—rather than drug prices generally, and it builds in exemptions for cost-justified increases and cheap generic competitors. Its main uncertainty is behavioral: companies could shift increases into new-drug launch prices or smaller repeated hikes. On balance it is a targeted deterrent with revenue diverted to research, and the main cost falls on companies profiting from spikes.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced on February 7, 2019, read twice, and referred to the Senate Finance Committee the same day, and no further action was ever taken before the Congress ended in January 2021.

narrative.text: Sen. Sherrod Brown introduced the Stop Price Gouging Act in the Senate on February 7, 2019, joined by Sens. Kirsten Gillibrand and Maggie Hassan as original cosponsors.
The bill was read twice and referred to the Committee on Finance on the day of introduction, and the action history shows no markup, hearing, or floor vote ever followed.
Five senators cosponsored the bill, all Democrats, and the bill never advanced out of committee during the 116th Congress.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Pharmaceutical companies that would have owed the excise tax on price-spike revenue are better off; no tax was enacted and no company had to report quarterly price data to the government.

for.role: U.S. Senator from Ohio; bill sponsor
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Stop Price Gouging Act and recruited cosponsors for it.

for.name: Sens. Kirsten Gillibrand and Maggie Hassan
for.role: U.S. Senators from New York and New Hampshire; original cosponsors

against.what_they_did: Never took up the bill; no markup, hearing, or vote was scheduled in the two years the committee held it.

sides.party_line_note: All six supporters in the Senate were Democrats and no Republican cosponsored the bill, and it died in a committee chaired by a Republican without ever reaching the floor.

industries.note: The bill would take 50% to 100% of the revenue a company gains from raising a drug's price faster than inflation, directly cutting into the profits that come from price spikes on drugs sold through Medicare, Medicaid, and other federal programs. Companies also would face quarterly public price reporting and per-day penalties for missing reports.

industries.industry: Health plans and pharmacy benefit managers
industries.note: The bill requires a GAO study of how drug manufacturers and health plans, including private insurers and Medicare and Medicaid, set initial launch prices for new drugs, but imposes no tax or requirement on them directly.
